Your brain runs on about twenty watts, roughly the power of a dim light bulb. A single A.I. accelerator draws about seven hundred. So how does a machine this frugal compute? Let's open it up the way an engineer would.

Imagine you are handed a bag with eighty-six billion parts that all look alike, and asked how a computer is built from them. An engineer would not study their shape. An engineer would ask three questions. How many inputs does a part have? How many outputs? And what does it put out?

The part is the neuron, and it is surprisingly simple. Thousands of wires come in. One wire goes out, but it branches like a tree, so the same signal reaches thousands of listeners. Inside, the neuron adds up what arrives. Some inputs push the sum up, others push it down. When the sum crosses a threshold, the neuron fires a short click, about a millisecond long. Every click is the same, so everything a neuron says is written in timing: how often it clicks, and when.

Where the wire meets a neighbour there is a tiny gap, and chemistry carries the signal across. The wire releases a transmitter, and the neighbour catches it. Here is the lucky part. Almost every neuron releases the same substance at all of its tips. So we can sort the bag by what each neuron releases, and name each type by the first four letters of its transmitter. Glutamate neurons are GLUT. Then GABA, DOPA for dopamine, SERO for serotonin, NORA for noradrenaline, and ACET for acetylcholine.

Sorted, the bag is lopsided. Out of every thousand neurons, about nine hundred and sixty are GLUT. They push the receiver toward firing: a plus. About thirty-six are GABA: a minus. Everything else together is a few neurons in a hundred thousand. A drop in the ocean.

But that drop is wired completely differently. GLUT and GABA neurons are like telephone lines: each wire goes to particular neighbours. The tiny DOPA, SERO, NORA and ACET groups are radio stations. Their wires spread across huge regions, and millions of cells hear the same message at once. The telephone network carries data. The radio carries settings: how loud everything is, whether to learn, whether it is time to sleep. Every computer is built this way: billions of memory cells, and a handful of control registers.

One subtlety. The molecule does not know whether it is a plus or a minus. It is a key. What happens is decided by the lock, the receptor on the receiving cell. The same dopamine excites one cell and quiets another, depending on which lock it carries.

The most famous radio channel is dopamine. What does it broadcast? Give an animal an unexpected drop of juice, and its dopamine neurons burst. Now light a lamp before every juice. The animal learns that the lamp predicts juice, and the burst moves to the lamp. And if the lamp comes but the juice does not, the dopamine neurons fall silent exactly when the juice was due. Dopamine does not say good. It says better than I expected: the same error signal that programs use to learn from their mistakes.

So the brain is a vast network of near-identical parts: pluses and minuses for data, and a few radio stations that tune the whole machine. Next time: what you can build from pluses alone.
